title: The US electrical grid from power plant to wall outlet
summary: One causal chain, start to finish: how a watt is made, stepped up, moved, stepped down, and delivered - and why every stage looks the way it does.

blocks.title: Follow one watt home
blocks.body: The North American grid is often called the largest machine ever built, and it runs with almost no storage: the power you use was generated a fraction of a second ago. This page walks the whole causal chain from a spinning generator to your wall outlet, and explains why each transformation exists.

blocks.heading: The whole chain in one look

nodes.title: Generation
nodes.detail: A turbine spins a generator; electricity is made at the moment it is needed.

nodes.title: Step-up transformer
nodes.detail: Voltage jumps to transmission levels so current - and loss - drops.

nodes.title: Transmission
nodes.detail: High-voltage lines move bulk power across regions.

nodes.title: Substation
nodes.detail: Voltage steps down to distribution levels near where power is used.

nodes.title: Distribution
nodes.detail: Pole and pad lines carry power through neighborhoods.

nodes.title: Service transformer
nodes.detail: The can on the pole drops 7,200 V to 120/240 V for a handful of homes.

nodes.title: Meter and panel
nodes.detail: The utility measures usage; the breaker panel splits it into circuits.

nodes.title: Outlet
nodes.detail: 120 V for most things, 240 V for the big loads.

blocks.heading: Stage one: making it
blocks.body: Almost all grid power starts as motion: steam spun by boiling water (coal, gas, nuclear, geothermal), falling water (hydro), wind, or gas turbines - with solar the notable exception, making DC directly from light. The generator converts that motion to three-phase AC at roughly 11 to 25 kV. Three-phase is used because it delivers steady power and creates the rotating magnetic fields motors want.

blocks.heading: Why the voltage goes up: the loss equation
blocks.body: Power loss in a wire is current squared times resistance. Move the same power at ten times the voltage and you need a tenth the current - and losses fall a hundred-fold. That single equation is the reason the grid's backbone exists: high voltage is not about power, it is about not heating the countryside with your electricity before it arrives.

blocks.heading: Stage two: stepping up
blocks.body: At the plant fence, a step-up transformer raises generator voltage to transmission level - anywhere from 138 kV to 765 kV on the big lines. Transformers only work on AC, which is a large part of why AC won the original current war: it can be transformed efficiently, and transformation is what makes long-distance power possible at all.

blocks.heading: Stage three: moving it
blocks.body: Transmission lines are the grid's highways, carrying bulk power between regions and from remote generation to cities. The continental US is not one grid but three big interconnections - Eastern, Western, and most of Texas - that run independently, joined only by a handful of DC ties. Inside each one, every generator spins in synchrony at 60 Hz, and that shared rhythm is what an operator means by grid stability.

blocks.title: There is no warehouse
blocks.body: Except for a small and growing amount of battery and pumped-hydro storage, supply must equal demand every second. When you flip a switch, a generator somewhere feels it instantly as a tiny extra load. Grid operators spend their day forecasting demand and scheduling generation to meet it; frequency drifting off 60 Hz is the visible symptom of imbalance.

blocks.heading: Stage four: stepping down
blocks.body: Near where power gets used, substations step transmission voltage down to distribution levels - commonly 4 to 35 kV. A substation is also a switchyard: breakers, buswork, and protection relays that can isolate a faulted line in cycles, so one tree branch does not darken a county. This is where the grid stops being a highway and becomes streets.

blocks.heading: Stage five: the neighborhood wires
blocks.body: Distribution feeders leave the substation at neighborhood voltage - 7,200 V to ground is common in the US - and run along poles or underground. This is the part of the grid you can see, and the part that fails most: squirrels, branches, and car-versus-pole all live here. Fuses and reclosers sectionalize faults so a problem on one street stays on one street.

blocks.heading: Stage six: the can on the pole
blocks.body: The final transformer - the gray can on the pole or the green box on the lawn - drops 7,200 V to 120/240 V split-phase for a handful of homes. Split-phase gives two 120 V legs of opposite phase; between either leg and neutral you get 120 V, and across both legs you get 240 V for the dryer, range, and EV charger. One failed can darkens a few houses, which is why those outages feel personal.

blocks.heading: Stage seven: into the house
blocks.body: The service drop (or lateral, underground) runs from the transformer through the meter - the utility's cash register - to the main panel. The panel's main breaker protects the service, and branch breakers split power into 15 and 20 amp circuits. Everything downstream of the panel is yours; everything upstream is the utility's. The meter is the border.

blocks.heading: The voltage ladder, rung by rung
rows: As high as generator insulation allows
High enough to beat I-squared-R losses over distance
Feeding substations and large industrial sites
Low enough to run through neighborhoods
Safe enough for homes, high enough for big loads
blocks.caption: Every step down trades efficiency for safety, one transformer at a time.

blocks.heading: Follow the watt, condensed
items: A gas turbine spins up because the evening forecast said you would cook dinner.
Its generator makes 18 kV three-phase AC; the step-up transformer raises that to 345 kV.
Transmission lines carry it eighty miles at a few percent loss.
A substation steps it to 7.2 kV and hands it to your street's feeder.
The pole can drops it to 120/240 V for your house and four neighbors.
The meter counts it, the panel splits it, and the outlet delivers it - generated less than a second ago.

blocks.heading: Check the reasoning
blocks.prompt: Why is long-distance transmission done at hundreds of kilovolts instead of at distribution voltage?
options: Higher voltage means lower current for the same power, and losses fall with the square of current
Higher voltage makes the electricity travel faster
blocks.explanation: Loss is I-squared-R. Ten times the voltage means a tenth the current and a hundredth the loss. Speed through the line is essentially the same either way.

blocks.heading: Check the map
blocks.prompt: The gray can on the pole fails at dusk. Roughly how many homes go dark?
options: A handful - it serves only the few houses fed from it
The whole neighborhood - it is the substation
Nobody - the grid reroutes instantly at that level
blocks.explanation: A service transformer feeds a small group of homes. Its failure is hyper-local - your street goes dark while the next street keeps its porch lights, which is exactly the pattern these outages show.
